content: Polywater was a hypothesized polymerized form of water that became the subject of significant scientific controversy in the late 1960s. Initially, it was believed to possess unusual physical properties, such as a higher boiling point, a lower freezing point, and a viscosity comparable to syrup. However, subsequent investigations revealed that polywater was an illusory phenomenon, and it is now regarded as a classic example of pathological science. The concept of polywater originated from the work of Soviet physicist Nikolai Fedyakin, who conducted experiments on water that had been condensed in or repeatedly forced through narrow quartz capillary tubes. Fedyakin's findings suggested the existence of a new form of water with anomalous properties. Boris Derjaguin, a prominent surface physicist in Moscow, refined Fedyakin's methods and was able to produce this mysterious substance more efficiently, albeit in small quantities. Derjaguin's research indicated that this anomalous water had a freezing point of −40°C or lower, a boiling point of 150°C or higher, a density of approximately 2 g/cm³, and an unusual thermal expansion behavior. Although these findings were initially published in Soviet scientific journals and summarized in English in Chemical Abstracts, they attracted little attention from Western scientists. This changed in 1966 when Derjaguin presented his work at the Discussions of the Faraday Society in Nottingham, England. Western scientists began to take notice, and by 1968, research on polywater was underway in both England and the United States. The phenomenon sparked a scientific frenzy, with some researchers successfully replicating Derjaguin's results while others failed. Various theories were proposed to explain polywater, including its potential impact on trans-Atlantic phone cables and the possibility that it could convert ordinary water into polywater, reminiscent of the apocalyptic scenario in Kurt Vonnegut's novel Cat's Cradle. Skepticism about polywater's authenticity grew, with concerns about contamination being a primary issue. Despite assurances in published papers about the meticulous precautions taken to avoid contamination, Denis Rousseau of Bell Labs conducted an experiment using his own sweat after a handball game and found that it exhibited identical properties to polywater. Rousseau subsequently published a paper suggesting that polywater was merely water contaminated with small amounts of biological impurities. This revelation prompted a new wave of more rigorously controlled experiments. When these experiments were conducted using thoroughly cleaned glassware, the anomalous properties of polywater disappeared. Chemical analyses consistently showed that polywater samples were contaminated with various substances, such as silicon and phospholipids, which accounted for the observed changes in physical properties. Electron microscopy further revealed the presence of small solid particles, explaining the increased viscosity. Ultimately, even the scientists who had initially supported the existence of polywater conceded that it was not a distinct form of water. In the Soviet Union, acceptance of this conclusion took longer, as some scientists continued to defend the idea. Denis Rousseau later used polywater as a textbook example of pathological science and wrote about other similar cases. In popular culture, polywater appeared in the Star Trek science fiction universe. It was featured in the original series episode The Naked Time and the Next Generation episode The Naked Now. In these stories, polywater was depicted as forming under extreme gravitational conditions, such as the breakup of a planet or the collapse of a red supergiant star into a white dwarf. When introduced into humanoid systems, polywater intoxication could occur, mimicking the effects of severe alcohol intoxication by acquiring carbon from the body and acting on the brain. It was also shown to interact with Soong-type androids with positronic brains, as seen in the contamination of the android Data in 2364. Within the series, this polywater intoxication was referred to as the Psi 2000 virus, named after the planet where it was first discovered, though it was not strictly a virus. Additionally, the story Polywater Doodle by Howard L. Myers appeared in the February 1971 issue of Analog Science Fiction/Science Fact.
